newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says time for Mobutu "dictatorship" is over.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says time for Mobutu "dictatorship" is over.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday signalled its desire that Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko step down, saying "the time for dictatorship is over" and the vast, rebellion-torn African nation should move toward democracy.
Spokesmen at the White House and the State Department were quick to insist they were not demanding that Mobutu resign. They said this was a decision for Zaire and its people.

But their comments nonetheless were clearly aimed at prodding Mobutu -- once treated as a strategic ally and a Cold War bulwark against communism in Africa -- to give up any hope of clinging to power.

"We do know one thing, we think the time for dictatorship is over in Zaire and the time for stability and democracy, if democracy can be achieved -- we think that time is approaching," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said it was time for an "orderly transition" in Zaire and that "we want everyone to cooperate to make that orderly transition possible."
"I think that it's clear that we have to move beyond President Mobutu and think about how we can structure a governemnt that will meet the needs of the Zairean people," McCurry said.
He admitted he was straddling a fine diplomatic line, telling reporters that "ambiguity is an art form."
The United States was braced for a possible evacuation of about 450 Americans from the country. U.S. troops were stationed in the region in case the call to evacuate came.
But McCurry added: "We are frankly satisfied so far that those types of measures are not necessary."

With rebel forces now holding nearly half of the sprawling nation, Mobutu, 66, suffering from prostate cancer but hanging onto power, has declared a state of emergency in Kinshasa and the rest of the country.
On Wednesday he appointed a senior general as prime minister, effectively replacing long-time opposition figure Etienne Tshisekedi who was named only last week.
Shots rang out in Kinshasa on Wednesday as security forces tried to break up a march by thousands of Tshisekedi's supporters, witnesses said.

McCurry said Washington believes negotiations on Zaire's civil war should lead to a ceasefire and a political settlement with an orderly transition to a new government and eventually, democratic elections.

McCurry said the U.S. position "clearly reflects our view that Mobutuism is about to become a creature of history, because the support for President Mobutu is not sufficient to lead Zaire into the next chapter of its history."
Asked whether the United States was actively involved in finding an exile home for Mobutu, he declined comment.

Pressed on whether it would be better if Mobutu were to go into exile, the White House spokesman replied: "There has to be ... some arrangements made for a transitional process that leads to a newly elected government."
He said the Mobutu government was "well aware" of the U.S. position.
The Washington Post quoted a senior U.S. official as saying the United States has been pressing its old Cold War ally to resign and go into exile to help achieve a peaceful settlement in the country.
It said the U.S. message has been conveyed to Mobutu in recent weeks by various African leaders including Morocco's King Hassan.

But the State Department's Burns waved aside a reporter's suggestion that Washington was declining to say publicly what it was telling Mobutu privately, saying, "The United States does not run around on a daily basis and advise governments to resign ... It's up to the Zairean people, its government, its opposition, to decide these questions."
